SET and a name with no = lists the variables whose names start with it. In the quoted form, the value ends at the last quote.SET /A's operators, the tightest first: ( ) grouping; ! ~ - (not, bitwise not, negation); * / % (in a batch file, %% for %); + -; << >> (shifts); & (and); ^ (exclusive or); | (or); = *= /= %= += -= &= ^= |= <<= >>= (assignments); and , between expressions. Any other word is a variable's name, its value read as a number (0 when it is not set). Numbers are decimal (17), hexadecimal (0x11) or octal (021). Quote an expression that holds & | ^ < or >. At the prompt, SET /A prints the last expression's value; in a batch file it prints nothing.SET /P with an empty line, or none, leaves the variable as it is and sets ERRORLEVEL to 1.Before a line runs, each %variable% in it is replaced by the variable's value. %variable:~offset,count% is part of the value: offset characters are skipped, then count kept (the rest without ,count). A negative offset counts from the end, and a negative count leaves out that many at the end.%variable:old=new% is the value with each old replaced by new, whatever the case of its letters; %variable:*old=new% replaces everything up to the first old.These names have a value even when no variable is set by them: %CD%, %DATE%, %TIME%, %RANDOM%, %ERRORLEVEL%, %CMDEXTVERSION% and %CMDCMDLINE%.␀␀␀ 2C␀␀␀␀½2C␀␀␀Ü4C␀Z␀␀␀65C␀$␀␀Z6C␀␀␀␀÷6C␀␀␀␀shift␀␀␀¸7C␀␀␀␀Moves a batch file's arguments down one: %1 takes %2's value, and so on.SHIFT [/n]␀␀8C␀
